name: Children & Youth Programming
description: Iranian programming for younger audiences includes dedicated broadcasting, animation, puppetry, educational material, and digital content. Its cultural significance extends beyond children’s entertainment, while evidence about audience reach and educational outcomes remains uneven.

seo.title: Children & Youth Programming in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iranian children's broadcasting, television puppetry, educational media, and the evidence needed to assess their reach and impact.

content.heading: A field spanning broadcasting and digital media
content.content:
Iran’s media for younger audiences combines television production with educational and digital work. A documented institutional example is the Children and Youth Broadcasting Center of Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting, or IRIB, the national state broadcaster. An August 2026 report by the ECO Cultural Institute describes a visit to the center at which its head presented television programmes, animation, digital content, and the activities of Pooya TV. The report establishes that these activities were being presented together within the center’s remit; it does not independently evaluate their quality or audience reach. [s1]

That distinction matters when reading descriptions of children’s media. A broadcaster’s commitment to educational or cultural programming describes its stated purpose. Demonstrating that a programme improves learning, reaches underserved audiences, or suits a particular developmental stage requires separate evidence. The visit report documents professional discussion about children’s development and family media literacy, rather than measured outcomes. [s1]

content.heading: Puppets, performance, and shared cultural references
content.content:
Television puppetry provides a distinctive entry into Iranian screen culture. Research at the University of Music and Performing Arts Graz examines how Iranian television puppets combine voice, movement, music, and dance. Its project description argues that puppet performance can operate with greater latitude than human performance in some areas of national television. This is a research framing about artistic practice, not evidence that puppeteers are free from editorial restrictions. [s2]

A useful example is Kolah Ghermezi, whose name means Red Hat. Cultural analysis published by Ajam Media Collective describes the puppet’s exchanges with Iraj Tahmasb’s adult presenter and the character Pesarkhaleh, a helpful cousin associated with everyday responsibilities. The article interprets the programme through humour, solidarity, and familiar domestic behaviour. Read as criticism rather than an audience survey, it helps explain how children’s television can also carry references that adults recognize. [s3]

Consequently, puppetry should not automatically be treated as preschool material. Its intended audience, language, humour, and social references need to be considered programme by programme. The Graz research focuses on performance practices, while the Ajam essay offers an interpretation of particular characters; neither supplies a national age profile of viewers. [s2][s3]

content.heading: Education and responsible representation
content.content:
Educational media belongs within a wider learning environment. In April 2022, UNICEF welcomed the resumption of in-person schooling in Iran after pandemic closures and emphasized catching up on lost learning and returning excluded children to classrooms. Its statement is a reminder that screen-based provision and classroom participation are different questions: the availability of remote material does not establish that every child can use it effectively. [s4]

UNICEF’s Iran country programme for 2017–2022 also identified public and media advocacy as an area of work, including strengthening media capacity in the ethical representation of children. This concerns how children are portrayed as well as what they watch. It provides a historical programme commitment, rather than a verified description of all current broadcaster practices. [s5]

content.heading: Looking beyond programme labels
content.content:
Advertising is another part of the viewing environment. A study published in the International Journal of Preventive Medicine examined food advertising during Iranian children’s television programmes using broadcasts sampled in 2007–2008. Its value here is methodological: it treats the commercial messages surrounding programmes as material that can be examined systematically. Its historical sample cannot describe today’s schedules, newer channels, or digital advertising. [s6]

A balanced account therefore separates production, distribution, representation, and impact. Iran’s documented programming institutions and performance traditions provide substantive material for cultural study. Claims about contemporary popularity, regional inclusion, accessibility, or educational effectiveness need programme-specific research rather than assumptions drawn from a channel name or a stated mission. [s1][s2][s5][s6]

name: Audiovisual Archives
description: Iran’s audiovisual heritage is held across film archives, broadcasting collections, and independent digital initiatives. Preservation, cataloguing, public access, and permission to reuse a recording are separate responsibilities that should not be inferred from the existence of an online copy.

seo.title: Audiovisual Archives of Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran's film and broadcast collections, independent digital archives, and the distinctions between preservation, access, and reuse.

content.heading: A heritage distributed across collections
content.content:
Iran’s audiovisual heritage does not belong to a single collection. Film preservation and broadcast archiving have distinct institutional histories. Encyclopaedia Iranica records the inauguration of Film-khana-ye Melli-e Iran, the National Film Archive, in December 1958, when Persian and foreign films were collected and screened regularly. The entry establishes an early institutional role combining collection with exhibition; it is not a current guide to the archive’s holdings or admission procedures. [s1]

Professional directories identify further points of reference. The International Federation of Film Archives lists the National Film Archive of Iran in Tehran. The International Association of Sound and Audiovisual Archives lists Islamic Republic of Iran Broadcasting under broadcast archives. These entries identify institutions within professional networks, but do not establish that every collection has a searchable public catalogue or that researchers can obtain unrestricted access. [s2][s3]

content.heading: Beyond a single institutional catalogue
content.content:
Independent digital projects offer another way to encounter historical material. Golistan describes itself as a virtual museum of Iranian performing arts covering 1880–1990. Its stated scope includes radio programmes and plays, regional music, recordings on 78-rpm discs, film, theatre, and printed material. The site organizes discovery through watching, listening, and reading, illustrating how performance history can be explored across formats rather than through cinema alone. [s4]

Its description of digitized, indexed, searchable assets is a statement about the portal’s own collection. It should not be read as a claim that all Iranian performance recordings survive there, or that it holds the best surviving version of every item. For researchers, the useful starting point is an identifiable recording with enough descriptive information to establish its relationship to a performer, programme, place, or production. Collection scope and national completeness are different matters. [s4]

content.heading: Why digitization is only part of preservation
content.content:
Audiovisual preservation involves both vulnerable carriers and the systems needed to interpret digital files. The Digital Preservation Coalition’s handbook explains that physical decay and obsolete playback technology threaten recordings, and that collections need documented preservation plans. This is general professional guidance, not an audit of Iranian repositories. It explains why placing a video online does not, by itself, demonstrate that its source material is securely preserved. [s5]

Original objects can also retain evidence absent from a digital transfer. An article in the IASA Journal distinguishes recorded content from information carried by an object’s material, form, and labelling. Such features can help reconstruct how a recording was made or used. Its argument for retaining original recordings and relevant playback equipment is particularly useful when considering tapes, discs, or other carriers whose physical characteristics contribute to interpretation. [s6]

For an Iranian radio programme, for example, the spoken content may be only one part of its historical value. The recording’s identity, version, associated documentation, and provenance determine what a researcher can responsibly infer. This is an application of the preservation principles above, rather than a claim that any particular Iranian archive currently follows or neglects them. [s5][s6]

content.heading: Reading access claims carefully
content.content:
Preservation, discovery, consultation, and reuse should be assessed separately. A directory entry confirms an institutional reference; an online catalogue helps locate material; a playable file allows some form of consultation. None of these alone supplies a complete account of preservation arrangements or reuse permissions. The professional listings and Golistan portal provide different kinds of access evidence and should be described accordingly. [s2][s3][s4][s5]

The most defensible overview is therefore a map of complementary collections and practices. Iran’s film archive history, broadcasting collections, and independent portals open different routes into recorded culture. Assessing what survives, what has been digitized, and what remains inaccessible requires collection-level evidence rather than a single national completeness claim. [s1][s2][s3][s4]

name: Digital Media
description: Iran’s digital media includes online journalism, social platforms, Persian podcasts, newsletters, video publishing, and specialist writing. Understanding this field requires distinguishing editorial production from distribution platforms and examining how filtering, network disruptions, and unequal access affect circulation.

seo.title: Digital Media in Iran: Formats, Platforms & Access | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iranian digital journalism, podcasts, social platforms, and video, with careful distinctions between publishing, audiences, and internet access.

content.heading: Content, platforms, and access
content.content:
Digital media is best understood through several separate questions: who produces a work, where it is published, how people discover it, and whether they can reach it. A podcast available through an international listening service, a domestically hosted video, and a news link shared through messaging do not necessarily face the same distribution conditions. Research on Iran’s internet documents why these distinctions matter: restrictions can target services or connectivity, and an apparently functioning connection does not establish unrestricted access to outside information. [s1][s2]

This section brings together online news outlets, social media, Persian podcasts, digital newsletters, video media, and specialist blogs. These are editorial and technical forms rather than a single industry with one audience measure. The distinction between an individual publication and its distribution service is particularly important: a platform carries material from many producers, while a publisher remains responsible for a particular editorial product. The ChannelB podcast listing offers a concrete example of a named production distributed through a separate listening platform. [s3]

content.heading: Different formats serve different purposes
content.content:
Online news requires attention to authorship, sourcing, updates, and corrections. Social circulation adds another layer: the account sharing a claim may not be its original publisher. A useful reading practice is to follow a shared item back to its original publication and distinguish reporting from commentary or promotional material. This is especially relevant in an environment where independent research documents censorship, content manipulation, and pressure on people publishing online. [s1]

Audio illustrates a different editorial form. ChannelB’s public listing identifies Ali Bandari as its author and describes the programme as telling true stories in Persian. Episode notes include writing, sound design, editing, artwork, music credits, and source lists. Those features make visible a production process that differs from a short news update. They also provide starting points for evaluating a particular episode’s evidence; the presence of a bibliography does not automatically verify every statement in the recording. [s3]

Video publishing also includes services based within Iran. Aparat’s own company profile describes video publication, management, and analytics services built around domestic infrastructure. This establishes how the company presents its role; its claims of market leadership are not treated here as independently measured audience rankings. A video platform’s service description should be distinguished from the editorial identity and reliability of any individual channel it hosts. [s4]

Newsletters and specialist blogs add further questions about attribution and continuity. For a newsletter, readers need to know who sends it, whether it contains original work or a selection of links, and whether earlier issues remain available. For specialist writing, expertise and traceable evidence matter more than the format alone. These are editorial criteria for exploring the branch, rather than claims that a verified national directory or representative audience study exists.

content.heading: Access conditions change over time
content.content:
The technical record shows why platform availability must be dated. A collaborative report involving OONI, IODA, M-Lab, Cloudflare, Kentik, Censored Planet, the Internet Society, and ARTICLE 19 examined disruptions surrounding the protests that followed Jhina Mahsa Amini’s death in September 2022. It combined different measurement approaches to investigate service blocking and network disruption. This is evidence about documented events and tested networks, rather than a permanent availability list. [s2]

Freedom House’s 2024 assessment, covering June 2023 through May 2024, described censorship, surveillance, pressure on online expression, and policies favouring domestic internet services. It also reported that circumvention could add cost and that disruptions varied geographically and over time. These findings help explain why a platform can remain culturally relevant despite access restrictions, and why publishing online does not guarantee equal opportunities to read, watch, or participate. [s1]

More recent original technical research examines nationwide shutdowns in January and March 2026. A preprint by Ali Sadeghi Jahromi and Jason Jaskolka combines routing information, active probing, and other perspectives to study the disruptions. It is useful evidence of measured network behaviour, but its preprint status and observation window should remain explicit. It does not establish the availability of every service on the editorial cutoff date. [s5]

content.heading: What audience numbers can and cannot show
content.content:
A subscriber count, a play count, and a population estimate measure different things. ChannelB’s listing, for example, displays platform-specific engagement counters; these are not a census of unique listeners in Iran. They cannot establish where all listeners live, how many use other applications, or how many completed an episode. No national audience estimate is derived from them here. [s3]

Network measurements require similar care. OONI’s guidance explains that its tools test particular websites and applications, and that analysis depends on the chosen test, network, and period. A failed or anomalous test needs interpretation; a set of tests is not a survey of media preferences. [s6]

The most useful way to explore Iran’s digital media is therefore to retain both editorial identity and distribution context. Ask what a publication contributes, what supports its claims, and what its audience measures actually describe. Then examine access as a dated, network-dependent condition. This approach preserves room for cultural discovery without treating visibility, reach, and reliability as interchangeable. [s2][s3][s6]
